milestones.name: ELIZA
milestones.note: Weizenbaum’s paper describes a keyword and transformation program whose DOCTOR script answers like a Rogerian therapist.

source.title: ELIZA: A Computer Program for the Study of Natural Language Communication Between Man and Machine (CACM 9(1), January 1966)

milestones.name: PARRY
milestones.note: Psychiatrist Kenneth Colby wrote PARRY to simulate a person with paranoid schizophrenia; his 1971 paper describes the model and quotes interviews with it.

source.title: Artificial Paranoia (Colby, Weber and Hilf, Artificial Intelligence 2, 1971)

milestones.name: PARRY encounters the DOCTOR (RFC 439)
milestones.note: RFC 439 records a session over ARPANET in which PARRY talks to ELIZA’s DOCTOR script.

milestones.name: A.L.I.C.E.
milestones.note: Wallace’s chatbot used AIML, an XML schema for conversation rules, and won the Loebner Prize in 2000, 2001 and 2004. Wallace’s own AIML set gives 1995 as the start; only Wikipedia gives a day.

source.title: Artificial Linguistic Internet Computer Entity - Wikipedia

milestones.name: Cleverbot
milestones.note: Rollo Carpenter launched Cleverbot as a web app in October 2008; his earlier chatbot Jabberwacky went online in 1997.

source.title: Cleverbot.com - a clever bot - speak to an AI with some Actual Intelligence?

milestones.name: IBM Watson (Jeopardy!)
milestones.note: Watson won the three-night Jeopardy! match with $77,147, ahead of Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter.

milestones.name: Siri (iPhone 4S)
milestones.note: Apple announced Siri with the iPhone 4S as an assistant you speak to in plain language.

milestones.name: Cortana
milestones.note: Microsoft unveiled Cortana, a voice assistant for Windows Phone 8.1 built on Bing, as a beta.

source.title: Cortana (yes!) and Many, Many Other Great Features coming in Windows Phone 8.1

milestones.name: Xiaoice
milestones.note: Microsoft first released Xiaoice in China on 29 May 2014; its paper calls it an empathetic social chatbot built for long conversations.

source.title: The Design and Implementation of XiaoIce, an Empathetic Social Chatbot

milestones.name: Amazon Echo / Alexa
milestones.note: Amazon launched Echo, a speaker that wakes to the word “Alexa”, at first by invitation only.

source.title: Forget Siri, Amazon now brings you Alexa

milestones.name: Tay
milestones.note: Tay went live on Twitter as @TayandYou, and Microsoft took it offline after a coordinated attack in its first 24 hours taught it offensive replies.

milestones.name: Tay taken offline
milestones.note: Microsoft apologized for Tay’s offensive tweets and said the bot was offline.

milestones.name: Google Assistant
milestones.note: Sundar Pichai introduced the Google Assistant at I/O as a two-way, conversational helper.

source.title: I/O: Building the next evolution of Google

milestones.name: Transformer ("Attention Is All You Need")
milestones.note: Vaswani and co-authors posted the paper that introduced the Transformer architecture; the paper released no trained weights. Date is the arXiv v1 date.

milestones.name: Google Duplex
milestones.note: Google unveiled Duplex, which holds natural-sounding phone calls to do narrow tasks such as booking appointments.

source.title: Google Duplex: An AI System for Accomplishing Real-World Tasks Over the Phone

milestones.name: BERT
milestones.note: The paper presents BERT, a bidirectional Transformer pre-trained for language understanding. Date is the arXiv v1 date.

source.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding

milestones.name: GPT-2 (announced, staged release)
milestones.note: OpenAI announced GPT-2 but held back the full model, releasing larger versions in stages over the year.

source.title: Better language models and their implications

milestones.name: T5
milestones.note: The paper treats every text task as text-to-text with one Transformer model. Date is the arXiv v1 date.

source.title: Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer

milestones.name: GPT-2 1.5B (full release)
milestones.note: OpenAI released the full 1.5B model after the 117M, 345M and 774M versions, saying it had seen no strong evidence of misuse.

milestones.name: Meena
milestones.note: Google described Meena, a 2.6B-parameter open-domain chatbot trained to predict the next token. Date is the arXiv v1 date.

milestones.name: GPT-3
milestones.note: The paper describes a 175 billion parameter model whose news samples human raters had trouble telling from human writing. Date is the arXiv v1 date.

milestones.name: LaMDA
milestones.note: Google introduced LaMDA, a language model trained on dialogue that can hold open-ended talks on many topics.

milestones.name: InstructGPT (RLHF)
milestones.note: OpenAI fine-tuned GPT-3 on demonstrations and then with reinforcement learning from human feedback; raters preferred the 1.3B InstructGPT to the 175B GPT-3. Date is the arXiv v1 date.

source.title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback (arXiv:2203.02155)

milestones.name: GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003)
milestones.note: OpenAI introduced text-davinci-003 on November 28, 2022, and two days later began calling these models GPT-3.5.

source.title: Let's discuss our experiences transitioning from text-davinci-002 to text-davinci-003

milestones.name: ChatGPT
milestones.note: OpenAI released ChatGPT to the public as a free chat product.

milestones.name: Bard (announced)
milestones.note: Google opened Bard, its conversational AI, to trusted testers and previewed AI features in Search.

source.title: An important next step on our AI journey

milestones.name: Bing Chat
milestones.note: Microsoft launched a limited preview of a new Bing and Edge that join search, browsing and chat.

source.title: Reinventing search with a new AI-powered Microsoft Bing and Edge, your copilot for the web

milestones.name: LLaMA
milestones.note: Meta released LLaMA in 7B, 13B, 33B and 65B sizes; the arXiv paper followed on 2023-02-27.

source.title: Introducing LLaMA: A foundational, 65-billion-parameter large language model

milestones.name: GPT-3.5 Turbo (ChatGPT API)
milestones.note: OpenAI opened the model behind ChatGPT to developers as gpt-3.5-turbo, at $0.002 per 1,000 tokens.

source.title: OpenAI launches an API for ChatGPT, plus dedicated capacity for enterprise customers

milestones.name: Claude and Claude Instant
milestones.note: Anthropic launched Claude for chat and API use, with Claude Instant as a faster, cheaper option.

milestones.name: ChatGLM-6B and ChatGLM-130B
milestones.note: Zhipu put ChatGLM-130B live on chatglm.cn and released a smaller open model, ChatGLM-6B, the same day.

source.title: ChatGLM: A Family of Large Language Models from GLM-130B to GLM-4 All Tools

milestones.name: GPT-4
milestones.note: OpenAI reported a large multimodal model that accepts image and text inputs. Date is the arXiv v1 date of the technical report.

milestones.name: Bard (early access)
milestones.note: Google began early access to Bard in the US and UK.

source.title: Try Bard and share your feedback

milestones.name: PaLM 2
milestones.note: Google unveiled PaLM 2 at I/O in four sizes and used it to power Bard and more than 25 other products.

milestones.name: Claude 100K context window
milestones.note: Anthropic grew Claude's context window from 9K to 100K tokens, about 75,000 words.

milestones.name: Falcon 40B
milestones.note: TII released the 40B model, trained on one trillion tokens, for research and commercial use, with 7.5B and 1.3B models and the RefinedWeb dataset.

source.title: Technology Innovation Institute launches open-source Falcon 40B AI model for research and commercial use

milestones.name: Function calling (gpt-4-0613, gpt-3.5-turbo-0613)
milestones.note: OpenAI added function calling to the Chat Completions API, with new versions of gpt-4 and gpt-3.5-turbo and a 16k gpt-3.5-turbo.

source.title: Function calling and other API updates

milestones.name: MPT-30B
milestones.note: MosaicML released MPT-30B, an open model licensed for commercial use and trained with an 8k context on H100 GPUs, plus Instruct and Chat versions.

source.title: MPT-30B: Raising the bar for open-source foundation models

milestones.name: Claude 2
milestones.note: Anthropic released Claude 2 with better coding, math and reasoning and longer inputs and outputs, via API and a beta chat site.

milestones.name: Llama 2
milestones.note: Meta and Microsoft launched Llama 2 as free for research and commercial use, under an Acceptable Use Policy.

source.title: Meta and Microsoft Introduce the Next Generation of Llama

milestones.name: Qwen (Qwen-7B)
milestones.note: The team released Qwen-7B and Qwen-7B-Chat on ModelScope and Hugging Face under the Tongyi Qianwen license; commercial use requires an application.

milestones.name: Claude Instant 1.2
milestones.note: Anthropic released a faster, cheaper Claude Instant with better math, coding, and reasoning through its API.

milestones.name: Code Llama
milestones.note: Meta released Code Llama, a Llama 2 model tuned for code, in 7B, 13B and 34B sizes, adding a 70B model on 2024-01-29.

source.title: Introducing Code Llama, a state-of-the-art large language model for coding

milestones.name: Falcon 180B
milestones.note: TII released Falcon 180B, a 180-billion-parameter open-weight model, on Hugging Face.

source.title: Spread Your Wings: Falcon 180B is here

milestones.name: GPT-4V (ChatGPT vision and voice)
milestones.note: OpenAI said ChatGPT could now take images and speak aloud, with GPT-4V rolling out to Plus and Enterprise users first.

source.title: ChatGPT can now see, hear, and speak

milestones.name: Mistral 7B
milestones.note: Mistral released a 7.3B model under the Apache 2.0 license.

milestones.name: Meta AI assistant
milestones.note: Meta launched Meta AI in beta, a chat assistant in WhatsApp, Messenger, and Instagram built on Llama 2 technology, with Bing search.

source.title: Introducing New AI Experiences Across Our Family of Apps and Devices

milestones.name: DeepSeek Coder
milestones.note: DeepSeek released DeepSeek Coder, its first open-weight code models; the paper followed on arXiv on 2024-01-25.

milestones.name: Yi-34B
milestones.note: 01.AI released the Yi-6B and Yi-34B base models as open weights.

milestones.name: Grok (Grok-1 beta)
milestones.note: xAI announced Grok, an early beta assistant built on Grok-1 with live X data, for a waitlist of US users.

milestones.name: GPT-4 Turbo
milestones.note: OpenAI unveiled GPT-4 Turbo at its first DevDay, with a 128,000-token context window and an April 2023 knowledge cutoff.

source.title: New models and developer products announced at DevDay

milestones.name: Claude 2.1
milestones.note: Anthropic released Claude 2.1 with a 200K-token context window, fewer false claims, and system prompts.

milestones.name: Gemini 1.0
milestones.note: Google introduced Gemini in three sizes, Ultra, Pro and Nano.

source.title: Introducing Gemini: our largest and most capable AI model

milestones.name: Mixtral 8x7B
milestones.note: Mixtral is a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 46.7B total parameters, 12.9B used per token, under Apache 2.0.

milestones.name: Phi-2
milestones.note: Microsoft released Phi-2, a 2.7B base model with no RLHF or instruction tuning, in the Azure AI Studio catalog.

source.title: Phi-2: The surprising power of small language models

milestones.name: DeepSeek LLM
milestones.note: The paper describes open 7B and 67B models. Date is the arXiv v1 date, not the earlier weights release.

source.title: DeepSeek LLM: Scaling Open-Source Language Models with Longtermism

milestones.name: GLM-4
milestones.note: Zhipu made GLM-4 (0116), with a 128K context, available through its API on bigmodel.cn.

source.title: ChatGLM: A Family of Large Language Models from GLM-130B to GLM-4 All Tools

milestones.name: OLMo
milestones.note: Ai2 released OLMo with its weights, training data, and training code all open.

milestones.name: Qwen1.5
milestones.note: Qwen released Qwen1.5 base and chat models from 0.5B to 110B; the blog is dated 2024-02-04, the GitHub README says 2024-02-05.

milestones.name: DeepSeekMath (GRPO)
milestones.note: DeepSeek released DeepSeekMath 7B and introduced GRPO, a variant of PPO for training math reasoning.

source.title: DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models

milestones.name: Gemini Advanced with Ultra 1.0 (Bard renamed Gemini)
milestones.note: Google renamed Bard to Gemini and launched Gemini Advanced, which gives access to Ultra 1.0, along with a mobile app.

source.title: Bard becomes Gemini: Try Ultra 1.0 and a new mobile app today

milestones.name: Gemini 1.5
milestones.note: Google introduced Gemini 1.5 and offered Gemini 1.5 Pro in limited preview with up to 1 million tokens of context.

milestones.name: Gemma
milestones.note: Google released Gemma 2B and 7B in pre-trained and instruction-tuned forms, with terms that allow commercial use.

source.title: Gemma: Introducing new state-of-the-art open models

milestones.name: Mistral Large
milestones.note: Mistral offered Mistral Large through la Plateforme and Microsoft Azure, not as open weights.

source.title: Introducing the next generation of Claude

milestones.name: Command R
milestones.note: Cohere released Command R, a model tuned for retrieval and tool use, with weights for research use.

source.title: Command R: Retrieval-Augmented Generation at Production Scale

milestones.name: Grok-1 (open weights)
milestones.note: xAI released the weights of the 314B mixture-of-experts Grok-1 base model under Apache 2.0.

milestones.name: DBRX

source.title: Introducing DBRX: A New State-of-the-Art Open LLM

milestones.name: Grok-1.5
milestones.note: xAI announced Grok-1.5, with better reasoning and a 128K-token context, for early testers and Grok users on X.

milestones.name: Command R+
milestones.note: Cohere released Command R+, a larger model for business retrieval and tool use, with weights for research use.

source.title: Introducing Command R+: A Scalable LLM Built for Business

milestones.name: GPT-4 Turbo with Vision (GA)
milestones.note: OpenAI made GPT-4 Turbo with Vision generally available in its API.

milestones.note: Meta released 8B and 70B models and said models over 400B were still training.

source.title: Introducing Meta Llama 3: The most capable openly available LLM to date

milestones.name: OpenELM

source.title: OpenELM: An Efficient Language Model Family with Open Training and Inference Framework

milestones.name: Phi-3
milestones.note: Microsoft released Phi-3-mini (3.8B) on Azure AI Studio, Hugging Face and Ollama, and announced Phi-3-small (7B) and Phi-3-medium (14B).

source.title: Introducing Phi-3: Redefining what's possible with SLMs

milestones.name: DeepSeek-V2
milestones.note: DeepSeek released DeepSeek-V2, a low-cost mixture-of-experts model; the arXiv paper is dated 2024-05-07.

milestones.name: GPT-4o
milestones.note: OpenAI’s new top model takes text, speech and video and became the model behind ChatGPT.

milestones.name: Gemini 1.5 Flash
milestones.note: Google announced Gemini 1.5 Flash at I/O as a fast model distilled from 1.5 Pro, in public preview; the API changelog dates the preview 2024-05-10 and GA 2024-05-23.

source.title: Gemini breaks new ground with a faster model, longer context, AI agents and more

milestones.name: Codestral
milestones.note: Mistral released Codestral, its first code model, a 22B open-weight model with its own API endpoint.

milestones.name: Qwen2

milestones.name: Apple Foundation Models (2024)
milestones.note: Apple described the on-device (about 3B) and server models behind Apple Intelligence at WWDC 2024.

source.title: Introducing Apple's On-Device and Server Foundation Models

milestones.name: DeepSeek-Coder-V2
milestones.note: DeepSeek moved its coder API to DeepSeek-Coder-V2 on 2024-06-14; the paper and open weights followed on 2024-06-17.

source.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro Tech Blog: Advancing Open Intelligence

milestones.name: GPT-6.1 Terra
milestones.note: OpenAI added gpt-6.1-terra, a fast mid-tier sibling of GPT-6.1 Sol.

milestones.name: LFM3
milestones.note: Liquid AI released LFM3, a family of about-2B models for text, vision, audio, and more, under a license free only below $10M revenue.

source.title: Introducing LFM3: Every Modality for Specialized Intelligence

milestones.name: Gemini 4 Carbon
milestones.note: Google announced Carbon as its strongest model, for cybersecurity and long tasks; at launch only some cyber defenders in its Fairwind Program could use it, and there was no public API.

milestones.name: ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base
milestones.note: Baidu released ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base, a 280B mixture-of-experts base model with 14B active, with weights on Hugging Face under its own license.

milestones.name: Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2
milestones.note: Anthropic released Fable 5.2 "for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work" at $8 / $40 per million tokens, and kept Mythos 5.2 for verified organizations. Its news post, "Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2", is dated Nov 9, 2026.

tells.tell: Reflects the user’s words back as a question
tells.example: WHAT WOULD IT MEAN TO YOU IF YOU GOT SOME HELP
tells.evidence: Weizenbaum’s sample dialogue shows ELIZA turning each input into a question by keyword match and pronoun swap, such as “My father” answered with “YOUR FATHER”.

source.title: ELIZA: A Computer Program for the Study of Natural Language Communication Between Man and Machine

tells.tell: Content-free filler when no keyword matches
tells.evidence: The paper says the reserved keyword NONE triggers stock content-free remarks such as “Please go on”, “That’s very interesting” and “I see”.

source.title: ELIZA: A Computer Program for the Study of Natural Language Communication Between Man and Machine

tells.example: I would rather not discuss that anymore.
tells.evidence: The RFC 439 transcript of PARRY talking to ELIZA’s DOCTOR shows PARRY steering to fixed worries, such as the mob, and closing topics it does not want.

tells.tell: Bland, looping text under likelihood decoding
tells.evidence: Holtzman et al. found that decoding by likelihood “leads to text that is bland and strangely repetitive” and proposed nucleus sampling as the fix.

source.title: The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration (arXiv:1904.09751, ICLR 2020)

tells.tell: Statistical sampling artifacts visible to readers
tells.evidence: GLTR applied baseline statistical methods to flag generation artifacts, and its overlay raised untrained humans’ detection rate of fake text from 54% to 72%.

source.title: GLTR: Statistical Detection and Visualization of Generated Text (arXiv:1906.04043)

tells.example: As of my last knowledge update in January 2022
tells.evidence: Wikipedia’s AI-writing guide lists “as of my last knowledge update” and “Up to my last training update” as 2022 to 2023 signs from models with fixed cutoffs such as GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.

tells.tell: “As an AI language model” refusal boilerplate
tells.example: As an AI language model, I can't directly add content to Wikipedia for you
tells.evidence: Wikipedia’s guide lists “as an AI language model”, “as a large language model” and “I’m sorry” as refusal signs, quotes a 2024 article edit, and says outright refusals have become rare.

tells.tell: “As an AI language model” leaked into bot tweets
tells.example: as an AI language model, I don't have to pay taxes
tells.evidence: Yang and Menczer searched Twitter for the phrase to find LLM-run accounts, identified a botnet of 1,140 accounts, and found that LLM content classifiers could not tell them from humans.

source.title: Anatomy of an AI-powered malicious social botnet (arXiv:2307.16336)

tells.tell: ChatGPT interface text pasted into papers
tells.evidence: Retraction Watch reported that Guillaume Cabanac had posted more than 30 papers on PubPeer containing “Regenerate response”, not counting predatory journals.

source.title: Signs of undeclared ChatGPT use in papers mounting (Retraction Watch)

tells.tell: “As an AI language model” in published papers
tells.example: As an AI language model, I
tells.evidence: The same Retraction Watch report says Cabanac had found the phrase “As an AI language model, I” in nine papers so far.

source.title: Signs of undeclared ChatGPT use in papers mounting (Retraction Watch)

tells.tell: Refusal message used as a product title
tells.example: I'm sorry but I cannot fulfill this request it goes against OpenAI use policy
tells.evidence: Futurism found Amazon listings, including a dresser, a lounger and a recliner, whose product names were ChatGPT refusal messages.

source.title: Amazon Is Selling Products With AI-Generated Names Like 'I Cannot Fulfill This Request It Goes Against OpenAI Use Policy'

tells.evidence: Gray found that between 2022 and 2023 “intricate” rose 117%, “commendable” 83%, “meticulous” 59% and “meticulously” 137% in Dimensions, implying at least 60,000 LLM-assisted 2023 papers (slightly over 1%).

source.title: ChatGPT 'contamination': estimating the prevalence of LLMs in the scholarly literature (arXiv:2403.16887)

tells.evidence: Liang et al. found “commendable”, “meticulous” and “intricate” 9.8, 34.7 and 11.2 times more likely to appear in a sentence in ICLR 2024 reviews, and estimated 6.5% to 16.9% of review text was substantially LLM-modified.

source.title: Monitoring AI-Modified Content at Scale: A Case Study on the Impact of ChatGPT on AI Conference Peer Reviews (arXiv:2403.07183)

tells.evidence: Liang et al. found these four words most over-used by LLMs relative to humans and saw them surge in arXiv CS abstracts from 2023, where up to 17.5% of papers were LLM-modified.

source.title: Mapping the Increasing Use of LLMs in Scientific Papers (arXiv:2404.01268)

tells.evidence: Kobak et al. found 2024 excess ratios of r = 28.0 for “delves”, 13.8 for “underscores” and 10.7 for “showcasing” across over 15 million PubMed abstracts, putting at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts as LLM-processed.

source.title: Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary (arXiv:2406.07016; Science Advances 2025)

tells.tell: Excess style verbs, not topic nouns
tells.evidence: Kobak et al. found that past excess words were mostly nouns (79.2% of content words), while of 379 excess style words in 2024, 66% were verbs and 14% adjectives.

source.title: Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary (arXiv:2406.07016; Science Advances 2025)

tells.tell: “delve” and 20 other focal words, linked to RLHF
tells.example: delve, intricate, underscore, boasts, garnered, realm
tells.evidence: Juzek and Ward identified 21 focal words that spiked in scientific English, found no cause in architecture or training data, and found evidence for RLHF by comparing Llama 2-Base with Llama 2-Chat.

source.title: Why Does ChatGPT "Delve" So Much? Exploring the Sources of Lexical Overrepresentation in Large Language Models (COLING 2025)

tells.tell: “delve” falls after it is called out
tells.evidence: Geng and Trotta found “delve” and other flagged words dropped in arXiv abstracts soon after they were pointed out in early 2024, while “significant” kept rising.

source.title: Human-LLM Coevolution: Evidence from Academic Writing (arXiv:2502.09606)

tells.evidence: Reinhart et al. found instruction-tuned models use present participial clauses at 2 to 5 times the human rate (GPT-4o 5.3 times) and nominalizations at 1.5 to 2 times (GPT-4o 2.1 times), with larger gaps than base models.

source.title: Do LLMs write like humans? Variation in grammatical and rhetorical styles (PNAS 2025; arXiv:2410.16107)

tells.evidence: Relative to human text, GPT-4o used “camaraderie” 162 times, “tapestry” 155 times and “palpable” 95 times as often; Llama 3 70B Instruct used “camaraderie” 24 and “palpable” 47 times as often, and “tapestry” was not a top word for any Llama.

source.title: Do LLMs write like humans? Variation in grammatical and rhetorical styles (PNAS 2025; arXiv:2410.16107)

tells.evidence: Shaib et al. found models produce part-of-speech templates more often than human references, and 76% of templates in model text appear in pre-training data, against 35% for human text.

source.title: Detection and Measurement of Syntactic Templates in Generated Text (arXiv:2407.00211, EMNLP 2024)

tells.evidence: Sun et al. trained a classifier that named the source model among ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and DeepSeek with 97.1% accuracy, driven by word-level distributions that survive rewriting.

source.title: Idiosyncrasies in Large Language Models (arXiv:2502.12150, ICML 2025)

tells.evidence: Paech et al. report that some slop patterns appear over 1,000x more often in LLM output than in human text.

source.title: Antislop: A Comprehensive Framework for Identifying and Eliminating Repetitive Patterns in Language Models (arXiv:2510.15061)

tells.tell: Long answers with lists, headers and bold
tells.evidence: LMSYS found length the largest style factor in Arena votes (coefficient 0.249), with markdown lists 0.031, headers 0.024 and bold 0.019 when both are controlled.

source.title: Does style matter? Disentangling style and substance in Chatbot Arena (LMSYS)

tells.evidence: Anthropic wrote that previous Claude models “often made unnecessary refusals” and that Claude 3 refuses harmless prompts much less often.

source.title: Introducing the next generation of Claude

tells.tell: Sycophancy, agreeing with the user’s view
tells.evidence: Sharma et al. found sycophancy across five assistants on four tasks, and found that humans and preference models sometimes prefer convincing sycophantic answers over correct ones.

source.title: Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models (arXiv:2310.13548)

tells.evidence: OpenAI rolled back a GPT-4o update that leaned on short-term feedback and called the result “overly flattering or agreeable”.

source.title: Sycophancy in GPT-4o: What happened and what we’re doing about it

tells.tell: Chat phrasing aimed at the user
tells.evidence: Wikipedia’s guide lists “I hope this helps”, “Certainly!”, “You’re absolutely right!”, “Would you like...” and “let me know” as signs, with examples from 2023 to 2025 and early 2026.
Wikipedia’s guide lists “boasts a”, “vibrant”, “nestled”, “in the heart of” and “renowned” as a 2023 to 2025 sign and says the tone became less common from around 2024.
Wikipedia’s guide lists “In summary”, “In conclusion” and “Overall” summaries as a historical sign common in 2023 output.
Wikipedia’s guide dates em dash overuse from 2022 to September 2026, saying LLMs use them where people would use commas, parentheses or colons.
Bloomberg’s Dave Lee wrote that ChatGPT uses the em dash liberally, which has made the mark read as a sign of AI text.

source.title: Is This a ChatGPT Hyphen — or Just Good Writing? (Bloomberg Opinion)

tells.tell: Em dashes now suppressible on request
tells.evidence: Engadget reported Sam Altman’s November 14, 2025 post that ChatGPT now obeys custom instructions to avoid em dashes.

source.title: OpenAI says ChatGPT will listen if you tell it not to use em dashes
